Meanwhile every busy system leans on a cache to keep hot rows near the code that wants them. A cache trades perfect freshness for raw speed, and that bargain, though modest, quietly shapes how large products actually feel to users.

However the hard part is not storing values; it is knowing when to drop them. Stale entries breed bugs that look random and stubbornly resist repair, so careful teams pair each cache with clear rules: short lifetimes, explicit purges on write, and version keys; without such rules, one cache slowly becomes a second, wrong database.

Along with such gains, a stalling load can inflict its own harm; familiar traffic storms follow such faults, and slow disk scans stack up until throughput drops. Warmup logic can limit rush, but no such gimmick is total.

Finally measure before you trust any cache, then measure again right after, because guessing about raw speed is never done.
